title: The New Covenant of the Spirit
english: … utterly easy to throw off and very readily spat out. And indeed God said somewhere, “This people draws near to Me with their mouth and honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me; in vain do they worship Me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8–9). But our Lord Jesus Christ writes His holy and divine laws for us on fleshly tablets of the heart, that is, on tablets that can feel (2 Corinthians 3:3). That is why He also said through the voice of the prophet Ezekiel, “And I will tear out their heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in My ordinances” (Ezekiel 11:19–20). If anyone, then, does not lean on the shadows given through Moses, and does not have the law written in ink as on tablets of stone, but within, in the mind, through the Spirit, he is a letter of Christ known by all men (2 Corinthians 3:2–3).
Volume 2, Discourse 1.
“Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God,” and so on (2 Corinthians 3:4).

Paul, knowing it well, ascribes the dignity of the apostleship not to human powers but to God, who is mighty in all things and who holds it out, through Christ the mediator, to those worthy to receive it. That is why he says that all good things come to the saints in Christ; for “every perfect gift is from above,” from “the Father of lights” (James 1:17). Yet He through whom all things are, and in whom all things are, is Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16). He mediates between us and God in the saving economy, yet He works all things from God the Father, since He is His very Wisdom and Power (1 Corinthians 1:24).

But what is the confidence through Christ toward God? Listen as he goes on to say, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to reckon anything as coming from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 3:5); for “all wisdom is from the Lord” (Sirach 1:1), as it is written; “but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:5–6).

And what is the letter? The type in the law, the things still carried out as in shadows. And the spirit is the power of the worship in Christ, which shows those who approach it through faith to be spiritual. As far as the type falls short of the truth, so far, I think, do those who serve it come behind those who minister the truth as priests. For Christ sprinkles us with His own blood, and not only for “the purity of the flesh,” as the rites of the law certainly did; rather He cleanses “our conscience from dead works” (Hebrews 9:13–14) and frees us from transgression. Besides this He also grants us the hope of life; for it is true that “whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (John 3:36). For He has promised also the resurrection of our very bodies, and their return to incorruption and to a life without end.
“For indeed what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, because of the glory that surpasses it” (2 Corinthians 3:10).

Again he brings the dignity of the divine apostleship back to its incomparable superiority. Having compared the two ministries and set out very well what is proper to each, he shows that the ministry in Christ through the Spirit is the more radiant. This is the aim of his thought in these words, but the saying is not phrased very clearly; for it seems somehow not very easy to see into, nor ready to hand even for those who wish to see it. For what does “What was glorified has not been glorified,” and what follows, mean? What he wants to show is something like this. Moses was indeed glorified, he says, as minister of the law that is being set aside; but the glory of the new proclamation, the proclamation in Christ, overcame the first and made it seem not to have been glorified at all. For just as, while night still remains and its darkness blackens this whole universe, the disk of the moon flashes out, as it were, and the chorus of the stars has its own glory, yet when the sun …
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing the comparison of the law to writing on stone from the previous section.
The words “This people draws near to Me” are Isaiah 29:13 in the Septuagint, in the form Matthew 15:8–9 quotes; Cyril gives them as spoken by God.
“Spirit” is written in lower case in 2 Corinthians 3:6 here because Cyril explains it at once as “the power of the worship in Christ”, set against the letter of the law.
“Volume 2, Discourse 1” is a heading of the printed text.
The section ends mid-sentence, in the comparison of the moon and stars to the sun; it continues in the next section.
The column numbers of the Migne printing (PG 74, 332–335) are left out of the text.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 2 Cor u02 rem early

title: The Veil Taken Away in Christ
english: … rises and spreads out the glory of its brilliance, the light of the moon is overcome by what surpasses it and seems, somehow, never to have shone at all. In the same way, I think, you will take the sense of the words before us. For “what was glorified,” he says, that is, the ministry of the law, though it received its glory from God, seems somehow not to have been glorified at all, because of the surpassing glory, the glory, that is, given to those who serve the divine proclamation of the gospel; for the lesser always somehow gives way to what surpasses it.

“For if what is being set aside came with glory, much more will what remains be in glory” (2 Corinthians 3:11). What is being set aside? The shadow and the law, that is, the type. And what remains? The decrees of God. So the shadow too was in glory, but the things of Christ are in a brighter glory; for they remain, since they will prevail over the whole world under heaven.

“Since, then, we have such a hope, we use great boldness” (2 Corinthians 3:12). What hope? That of being made sufficient by God and fully fitted through grace to be “ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter” (2 Corinthians 3:6). It befits such men to speak with great boldness, ashamed neither of the weakness of the types nor of the lack of learning in their hearers; for the Holy Spirit, settled in the souls of the faithful, makes them understand with ease even the deep sayings.

“And not as Moses, who put a veil over his face” (2 Corinthians 3:13). In this too, again, the disciples of Christ are brighter in glory, because the word of their preaching was clear and not to be withstood, and had nothing hard in it, as the word through Moses did. For since the sons of Israel had proved unworthy, making the calf after so many wonders (Exodus 32:4), Moses put a mask over himself (Exodus 34:33), and in speaking the divine law to them he used veils, teaching through riddles. For they would not have been able to see the true face of the law, that is, Christ, but could barely approach, as it were, a second face, the shadow, which has no glory; and this, the shadow and the type, is being set aside. For it has ceased now that the new covenant has been brought in, and Christ is the end of the law that is being set aside (2 Corinthians 3:13; Romans 10:4).

So the hidden glory of Moses, Christ, was the end of the law that is being set aside. For if anyone takes away the shadow and strips off, as it were, the outward and second face, the face in the letter, he will see Emmanuel taking shape in many ways in each one, enduring slaughter for the world and saving all under heaven, so that He may be glorified by us and worshiped by the holy angels. So the light of the Savior’s glory is beyond the reach of Jewish minds. For since all spiritual contemplation looks to the mystery of Christ, and the unhappy Jews do not accept faith in Him, the veil has remained upon them, though it is set aside in Christ (2 Corinthians 3:14).
“But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16).

The Lord Himself is the light, and He “reveals the deep and hidden things” (Daniel 2:22); He shows the true and glorified face of the law to the wise, who are sanctified in the Spirit and made radiant through faith in Christ. For the law leads us like a tutor to Christ (Galatians 3:24); and one appointed to lead others to someone else does not have his pupils stop at himself, but rather carries them on to something better and greater than himself. That is why the inspired Paul says that he counted the things in the law as rubbish “because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ” (Philippians 3:8).

“Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17). We must therefore become spiritual, for in no other way is it possible to behold Christ, who is “the end of what is being set aside” (2 Corinthians 3:13), I mean the law. Then “the veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16) wholly and completely, and they will see holy Moses with his face bare and uncovered, no longer wearing the mask that comes from the letter, that is, the shadow cast by the …
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, finishing the comparison of the moon and stars with the rising sun from the previous section.
“Since they will prevail”: the Greek has εἰ (“if”), taken here as giving a reason, not as a doubt.
“Not to be withstood” renders ἀνυπόστατος, which can also mean “without substance”; the sense of the passage requires “irresistible”.
Christ as “the end of the law” is Romans 10:4, joined here with Paul's “what is being set aside” (2 Corinthians 3:13).
The section ends mid-sentence; “no longer wearing” carries the negation that stands at the start of the next section, where the sentence is finished.
The column numbers of the Migne printing (PG 74, 336–337) are left out of the text.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 2 Cor u02 rem mid

title: From Glory to Glory through the Spirit
english: … outward narrative. For among these are those in Christ who have richly received the free revelation of the Spirit. And if wherever the Spirit is, there freedom surely is as well (2 Corinthians 3:17), how is the Spirit not free by nature? If that is so, the Spirit stands outside the bounds of slavery and is no longer something created, but would rightly be ranked with the highest and free nature, to which power over all things belongs. For the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father, reaching out from Him to the creation in Christ.

“And we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Moses put a veil over himself because the sons of Israel could not look upon “the glory of his face” (2 Corinthians 3:7, 13), for they were unspiritual and fleshly and immature in faith. But we believers, whose heart has been enlightened by the torch the Spirit carries, and whose mind’s eye knows how to see purely, have beheld the Lord with unveiled face. For He has spoken to us and has been seen in glory and in a majesty most worthy of God; for we have known Him as God, the exact imprint of the Father’s being (Hebrews 1:3).

As in a mirror, then, we behold the divine and ineffable nature. For the mind of believers is, as it were, remolded from its schooling in the law into the teaching of the gospel, and is in a certain way transformed into spiritual knowledge. It does not settle for shadow or types, but has chosen to pass from the glory that belongs to the law to another glory, the glory in Christ, through the Spirit. So we are transformed into the same image. For as we carry the types over into truth, and out of the shadow in the law give shape to the mystery of Christ by the fine discernment of our thoughts, we shall find the same glory as if in plain sight. For if glory was given to those who served the law, greater still, and beyond all comparison surpassing the first, is the glory of the holy priestly ministers, who are also made sufficient by God as ministers “of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

It is plain, surely, and obscure to no one at all, that those who are moved from training in the law to the precision of the gospel would by all means be understood to be going, as it were, from the first glory to another glory, and to be remolded, so to speak, toward better things. And what moves them to this is the Spirit, who sets them free from the slavery that comes from the law; for in the Spirit “we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15) as sons and as free.

There is no other way to see the depth beneath the spare wording of the law except through the Holy Spirit alone; for it is the Spirit who searches “even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). By “the depths of God” we say is meant the knowledge stored up like treasure in the sacred writings. That is why the inspired David made his prayers to God, saying, “Unveil my eyes, and I will perceive Your wonders out of Your law” (Psalm 119:18). And the Savior Himself regarded with no small admiration the one who rises from knowledge of the law to spiritual knowledge, that is, the knowledge of the gospel. For He said, “Therefore I tell you that every scribe who has been made a disciple for the kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who brings out of his treasure things new and old” (Matthew 13:52). The old are the things in the law; the new are the things in Christ.

But if someone wishes the transformation of our same image from glory to glory to be understood in another way as well, he will take some such thought to mind: all of us who have known Christ and have been counted among the children of God are by all means in glory; but it is at the time of the resurrection that we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:18). For Christ Himself, who to us “the pledge of the …” (2 Corinthians 5:5)
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: the first words, ἐμφανοῦς ἱστορίας οὐκ ἔχοντα, finish the last sentence of the previous section (“they will see holy Moses … no longer wearing the mask that comes from the letter, that is, the shadow cast by the outward narrative”). The negation οὐκ ἔχοντα is carried there in “no longer wearing”, so the join reads cleanly.
Ends mid-sentence inside 2 Corinthians 5:5 (“the pledge of the …”); the next section opens with “Spirit” and finishes the sentence. No verb is supplied here.
εἰσὶ γὰρ ἐν τούτοις may mean “among these [who see Moses unveiled] are …” or “in these words are meant …”; it is rendered “among these are”, the plainer reading.
Πνεῦμα is neuter; to avoid an “it” that sounds impersonal and a “He” that the Greek does not mark, the noun “the Spirit” is repeated where English needs a pronoun.
γενητὸν μὲν οὐκέτι: “is no longer something created”, the logical “no longer” of the argument (if free by nature, then not among originated things).
ἰσχνότης τῶν ἐννοιῶν / ἰσχνολογία: “fine discernment of our thoughts” and “spare wording” (the terse, close-packed letter of the law), not “weakness”.
ἱερουργῶν: “priestly ministers”; Cyril uses ἱερουργός of the apostles, and later calls Paul “the priest of the divine mysteries” (ὁ τῶν θείων μυστηρίων ἱερουργός).
ἐποιεῖτο … οὐκ ἀθαύμαστον: litotes, “regarded with no small admiration”.
Possible allusions not cited inline: ὡς ἐν ἐσόπτρῳ θεωροῦμεν may echo 1 Corinthians 13:12; λελάληκε γὰρ ἡμῖν may echo Hebrews 1:2.
Psalm 119:18 is Psalm 118:18 in the Greek Septuagint numbering.

The argument about the Spirit and freedom at the head of this section reappears, nearly word for word, at the head of the next; both are translated as they stand. The column numbers of the Migne printing (PG 74, 338–339) and the page number 8 are left out of the text.
Divine pronouns are capitalised for clarity (He/Him/His for Christ and God).
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 2 Cor u02 rem close
